text: Microsoft 365 co-pilot agents are reusable mini assistants you can configure for a specific workflow. Instead of explaining the same task every time you start a new chat, you can give the agent a clear role, standing instructions, selected knowledge sources, and access to relevant work content. Think of it as turning a strong prompt into a reusable assistant. For this demo, I'll use the Microsoft 365 co-pilot app. In the left side panel, I click agent, then choose new agent. Here, I can describe the agent I want to create or go directly to the configuration. I'm going to build an assistant that helps me write weekly leadership updates. I'll call it Larry and give it a simple description. Helps me write weekly leadership updates. Next, I move to instructions. This is where I define how Larry should work. For this example, I'll paste in a prompt I've already tested. It defines the role, objective, rules, and output format. What changes each week is the input I give Larry, such as my notes, priorities, metrics, or meeting context. There's also a suggest improvements option that can help refine the instructions. Next comes knowledge. This is where I decide what information Larry can use. There are three main sources of knowledge I can add. The first is work content. This gives the agent access to information from my organization's workspace, such as cloud files, outlook, teams, and other connected sources. I can turn these sources on or off depending on what Larry actually needs. The second is web search. This allows the agent to use information from the public web. Because this brings public information into the workflow, be intentional about when you turn it on, especially if the agent is also working with internal or sensitive information. Follow your organization's policy on web-enabled AI features and what information is appropriate to use. For an internal leadership update like Larry, I may leave web search off if public information isn't needed. The third is attachments. This lets me upload information directly from my own device when I want Larry to work with a specific file. There is also a separate knowledge settings area. This is where I can configure some of the agent's capabilities. For example, I can allow it to use people data, create documents, charts, and code, or create images. I can also choose discourage model knowledge, which tells the agent to rely more heavily on the sources I've selected rather than on its general model knowledge. Once the knowledge setup is in place, I can add starter prompts so people can immediately understand how to use the agent. For example, draft this week's leadership update from my notes. That makes it clear what Larry is designed to help with. Before I finalize it, I choose preview and test Larry with a realistic example. I add this week's notes, priorities, blockers, and key updates. Larry generates a draft. Now I check three things. Does it follow the structure I asked for? Is it focused enough for a leadership audience? And does it accurately reflect the information I provided? If not, I refine the instructions or sources and test again. The goal isn't simply to create an agent. The goal is to create one whose output I can reliably use. Once I'm satisfied, I click create. The agent starts as private, and depending on my organization's settings, I may be able to share it with specific users or more broadly. Once created, I can reuse Larry directly in Microsoft 365 Copilot instead of rebuilding the workflow each week. The exact options you see may vary depending on your Microsoft 365 license, permissions, and admin settings. And if you need more advanced automation, actions, or integrations, that's where Copilot Studio comes in.
